content:
Hi,

I'm just getting started with Lean (still very much a beginner, so quite possible I'm missing something which should be obvious). I'm using Claude Code within VSCode with lean-lsp-mcp installed.

I find that Claude Code continually complains about stale diagnostics. Here are a few examples:

The coercion works — the earlier IDE errors were just stale diagnostics before the rebuild. Now let me update Main.lean to use the terser syntax and verify the full build.

These are stale diagnostics again (Main.lean depends on Html which just got rebuilt). Let me rebuild and confirm.

That's just an IDE staleness notice. Let me add a #guard test for documentPretty and then rebuild.

This kind of thing is happening almost all the time. Is this expected? Or does it suggest that there's something wrong with my setup? How might I diagnose what's going on if there is?

Many thanks in advance for any suggestions.
Why don't you just ask Claude this question? I have never seen this with Claude in VS Code so my guess is that the problem is at your end.

Good point. Apologies for not thinking of it myself.

This is what Claude says:

Two different things got conflated here, worth separating:

  • lean-lsp-mcp is the MCP server (mcp__lean-lsp__* tools) — I didn't invoke any of those tools in this session at all. All my verification went through lake build directly via Bash.
  • The "Imports are out of date and must be rebuilt" message came from a different channel: the PostToolUse:Edit hook, which reflects VS Code's built-in Lean4 extension and its live editor-side LSP session for the file you have open.

That message is accurate, not stale or wrong — it's the editor telling you its in-memory elaboration of Html/Document.lean hasn't reprocessed yet because I'd just edited Html/Node.lean (one of its imports) moments earlier on disk. That's expected and routine any time you edit a dependency out from under an open file; the editor's LSP session needs to re-elaborate, and until it does, it correctly flags itself as behind. It isn't a claim about correctness of the code.

Where I was sloppy: I said "that's just IDE staleness" and moved on without spelling out why that's a safe call. The actual justification is that lake build — the compiler, not the editor's incremental session — is ground truth, and I ran it immediately after and it passed cleanly with no errors from Document.lean. So the message resolved itself once the real build reprocessed the file; it wasn't masking anything. I should have said that explicitly instead of a one-line dismissal.

So I guess that's nothing to be worried about (and probably wouldn't happen if I was using Claude without IDE integration?). But I'm surprised that its not actually using the MCP at all. I've double-checked and it's definitely installed, enabled, and connected.

And here's what Claude says about that:

No CLAUDE.md or .claude/ config exists in this repo, so there's no standing instruction pointing me at lean-lsp-mcp — I never called ToolSearch for it this session, which is why it never got loaded.
Why I defaulted to lake build/grep:

  1. My task was multi-file (rewriting Node's representation, adding functions across Node.lean/Document.lean/Html.lean, editing markdown). lake build checks the whole project — including every #guard — in one shot. That's a better fit than lean-lsp-mcp's tools, most of which are scoped to a single file or cursor position (lean_goal, lean_hover_info, lean_diagnostic_messages for one file).
  2. The PostToolUse:Edit hook already fed me <ide_diagnostics> automatically after every edit — effectively lean_diagnostic_messages for free, without me having to call anything. That closed the gap where I'd otherwise have reached for the MCP.
  3. grep for documentPretty was searching plain text across .lean doc-comments and a .md file. lean-lsp's search tools (lean_references, lean_local_search) resolve real Lean declarations — they wouldn't see prose in a markdown file at all, and once I'd renamed the function there was no declaration left to search for.
  4. The MCP's own instructions flag lean_build as "SLOW! Only if needed" — reinforcing that a full-project check was meant to go through plain lake build, not the MCP.
    Where that reasoning was weaker: the termination-proof failure on renderPrettyInto (the sizeOf/decreasing_by issue) is exactly the kind of interactive, single-point problem lean_goal/lean_multi_attempt/lean_diagnostic_messages are built for. I hand-derived the fix and confirmed it via a full rebuild instead of exploring it interactively — that's a real spot where the MCP would likely have been faster.
    How to get me to use it: either tell me explicitly in the moment, or — since this is a standing preference, not a one-off — I can save it as a memory now (e.g. "prefer lean-lsp-mcp tools for single-file diagnostics/goal-state work; reserve lake build for whole-project verification") so I default to it in future sessions without you repeating yourself. Want me to save that?

And for completeness, here's what I've ended up putting in CLAUDE.md. Does this seem reasonable? Anything missing?

Verifying Lean changes

  • After editing a .lean file, verify it with mcp__lean-lsp__lean_diagnostic_messages (or other lean-lsp-mcp tools — e.g. lean_goal/lean_multi_attempt for interactive proof/termination work).
  • Ignore the editor's <ide_diagnostics> hook output.
  • Before considering a task complete, run lake build from the repo root as the final ground truth.
  • If a change adds or removes an import, use mcp__lean-lsp__lean_build instead of (or in addition to) plain lake build.

Please stop posting large amounts of AI-generated text. This text is written for you (and paid for by you), I don't think anyone else is interested in it. Read it or throw it away. If you don't understand any of it then ask the LLM more. Your set-up is your problem. The entire area is a big experiment right now and there are no right or wrong, or even standardised, answers about how to set things up. If you're not happy with your set-up and can't figure out how to fix it then uninstall everything and start again.
Apologies, I allowed myself to get carried away. Thanks for calling me out.
